sec.title: Background:
sec.p: Diabetic nephropathy is one of the most prevalent consequences of diabetes and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality in diabetic patients. The pathogenesis of Diabetic Nephropathy is very complex and is still not fully understood, resulting in poor therapeutic outcomes. Dapagliflozin is thought to be associated with decreased progression of diabetic nephropathy. However, fewer trials have been conducted for the role of dapagliflozin in human patients with diabetic nephropathy. This is the first systematic review and meta-analysis where we aim to generate appropriate evidence regarding the safety and efficacy of dapagliflozin in diabetic nephropathy.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: We searched the databases like PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) and Embase for studies published from inception to November 2023. Bias assessment was done using risk of bias tool for randomized controlled trial (RCT) and Newcastle-Ottawa scale for non-randomized studies. Synthesis of the data was done using RevMan 5.4 software. Efficacy was assessed in terms of lowering HbA1c level, serum creatinine, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio. Statistical heterogeneity was measured by using the I squared test and the results were reported using forest plots.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Two studies were selected, 1 RCT and 1 comparative study including 296 patients. The dapagliflozin-treated group showed significant improvements in lowering serum creatinine [Standardized mean difference (SMD): −0.56 (−1.08, −0.04), P < .00001] and HbA1c [SMD: −0.84 (−1.07, −0.61), P = .03] when compared to the control group. But there was no discernible change in urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio [SMD: −1.45 (−3.33, 0.42), P = .13] after dapagliflozin therapy. Hypoglycemia [risk ratio: 0.26 (0.08–0.82), P = .02] was considerably lower in the dapagliflozin treatment group than in the control group in terms of safety.

sec.title: Conclusion:
sec.p: This meta-analysis showed that dapagliflozin was more effective in treating diabetic nephropathy while having fewer side effects. Our results support to the endeavor of conducting bigger, multicentre RCTs that assess dapagliflozin’s efficacy and delineate its unfavorable risk profile.
Keywords: cardiovascular outcomes, dapagliflozin, diabetic nephropathy, meta-analysis, renal outcomes, SGLT2 inhibitor

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a predominant microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus and stands as a major contributor to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) globally. This condition is marked by persistent albuminuria, a progressive decline in glomerular filtration rate (GFR), and heightened cardiovascular risk, significantly impacting morbidity and mortality rates in diabetic patients.[1] Despite considerable progress in diabetes management, effective therapeutic interventions to slow or reverse DN remain inadequate, highlighting the need for continued exploration of innovative treatments.

Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have emerged as a promising therapeutic class for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). By inhibiting glucose reabsorption in the kidney’s proximal tubules, SGLT2 inhibitors reduce blood glucose levels independently of insulin.[2] Beyond their glycemic benefits, SGLT2 inhibitors, including dapagliflozin, exhibit potential renal and cardiovascular protective effects, making them an area of interest for DN management.[3]

Dapagliflozin, specifically, has shown efficacy in enhancing glycemic control and reducing cardiovascular events in diabetic patients.[4] Emerging evidence suggests that dapagliflozin may also confer renal protective effects, potentially mitigating the progression of DN.[5] However, the precise impact of dapagliflozin on renal outcomes in DN remains underexplored, with limited randomized controlled trials (RCTs) addressing this issue directly.

Given the limited but growing body of evidence, this systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in patients with DN. By synthesizing data from available studies, we seek to provide a comprehensive assessment of dapagliflozin’s role in managing DN, focusing on key outcomes such as changes in estimated GFR (eGFR), urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR), serum creatinine, glycemic control, and safety profiles. Our goal is to generate robust evidence that can inform clinical decision-making and guide future research in this critical area of diabetic care.

sec.title: 2.1. Research framework
sec.p: The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and Cochrane handbook of systematic review. The PRISMA flow diagram was used to illustrate the study selection process.[6,7]

sec.title: 2.2. Search strategy
sec.p: We conducted a comprehensive literature search to identify relevant RCTs comparing dapagliflozin with placebo in patients with DN. The databases searched included PubMed, MEDLINE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Embase. The search strategy employed the following keywords: “Dapagliflozin,” “SGLT-2,” “Diabetic Nephropathy,” and “Diabetic Kidney Disease.” The search was limited to studies published from inception to November 2023. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were manually searched to identify any additional studies.

sec.title: 3.1. Inclusion criteria
sec.p: Study Design: RCTs, comparative studies.
Population: Adults aged 18 years or older with a diagnosis of DN.
Intervention: Dapagliflozin treatment.
Comparison: Placebo or standard care.
Outcomes: Studies reporting on at least one of the following outcomes: eGFR, UACR, serum creatinine, HbA1c levels, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, and adverse events.
Language: Articles published in English.

sec.title: 3.2. Exclusion criteria
sec.p: Cross-sectional studies, case reports, and review articles.
Studies involving pediatric populations.
Studies without a placebo or standard care comparison group.
Studies not reporting relevant outcomes.

sec.title: 3.3. Research selection process
sec.p: Two independent reviewers screened the titles and abstracts of all identified studies. Full-text articles were retrieved for those meeting the inclusion criteria or for which relevance was uncertain. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer.

sec.title: 3.4. Data extraction
sec.p: Two review authors independently extracted the data. We gathered the following information from the eligible study.

list-item.p: 1) Study characteristics (author, year, country, sample size, duration)
2) Participant characteristics (age, sex, baseline renal function, diabetes duration)
3) Intervention details (dosage, frequency, duration, number of subjects)
4) Outcome measures (eGFR, UACR, serum creatinine, HbA1c, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, adverse events)

sec.title: 3.5. Assessment of risk of bias
sec.p: The Newcastle-Ottawa scale (NOS) for non-randomized studies was employed to rate the research quality. The NOS is a method of rating studies in which points are assigned depending on the degree to which a researcher’s objectives are met in the 3 distinct domains of selection, compatibility and outcomes.[8] Two researchers carried out the scoring. The final steps were to calculate the overall score with 7 to 9 being regarded as a good-quality study with low chance of bias, 4 to 6 as a high risk of bias and 0 to 3 as an extremely high risk of bias. Any disagreement that arose during the risk of bias assessment were resolved by supervisor. For randomized studies, the quality was appraised using the Rob2 and Cochrane Risk of Bias tools. To assess publication bias, we looked at the symmetry of funnel plots for each outcome.

sec.title: 3.6. Synthesis of included studies
sec.p: Data synthesis and meta-analysis were performed using RevMan 5.4 software. Continuous outcomes (e.g., eGFR, UACR, serum creatinine, HbA1c) were expressed as standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Dichotomous outcomes (e.g., all-cause mortality, cardiovascular events, adverse events) were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I2 statistic.[9] An I2 value >50% indicated significant heterogeneity, and a random-effects model was used; otherwise, a fixed-effects model was applied.[10]

sec.title: 3.7. Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the results by excluding studies with high risk of bias, small sample sizes, or short duration of follow-up. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger test if more than 10 studies were included in the meta-analysis.[11]

sec.title: 4.1. Study selection
sec.p: A total of 200 potential articles were found in the preliminary electronic search of the databases. Following elimination of the duplicate articles, the remaining articles were screened based on title, abstract and full text. The details of the study selection are shown in Figure 1.

sec.title: 4.2. Study characteristics
sec.p: In this meta-analysis, 2 studies are included. One study is RCT published in 2022 while another study is retrospective comparative study published in 2023.[12,13] The study included 296 patients from 2 separate Randomised Control trials. sec.p: Efficacy: The efficacy of dapagliflozin is measured in terms of HbA1c level, serum creatinine and Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio.

HbA1c level: There was significant heterogeneity in the analysis of 2 studies (I2 = 79%, P = .03), so, random effect model was used for the analysis. The analysis reported significant decrease in HbA1c level in the dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls (pooled SMD −0.56; 95% CI [−1.08, −0.04]; P overall effect = .03) (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Forest plot showing HbA1c level in the dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls.

sec.p: Serum creatinine level: For the analysis of serum creatinine level, significant heterogeneity wasn’t observed (I2 = 26%, P = .24), therefore, fixed effect model was used for the analysis. There was significant decrease in serum creatinine level in experimental group compared to controls (pooled SMD −0.84; 95% CI [−1.07, −0.61]; P overall effect < .00001) (Fig. 3).

caption.p: Forest plot showing creatinine in the dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls.

sec.p: UACR: In the analysis of serum creatinine level, significant heterogeneity wasn’t observed (I2 = 98%, P < .00001), therefore, random effect model was used for the analysis. There was insignificant change in UACR in dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls (pooled SMD −1.45; 95% CI [−3.33, 0.42]; P overall effect = .13) (Fig. 4).

caption.p: Forest plot showing UACR in the dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls. UACR = urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio.

sec.p: Safety: The incidence of side effects like hypoglycemia, hypotension, dizziness, UTI, DKA were comparably lower in the dapagliflozin treated group than controls. In the analysis of incidence of hypoglycemia among dapagliflozin treated group, no heterogeneity was observed (I2 = 0%, P = .65), so, fixed effect model was used for the analysis. The analysis reported significant incidence of hypoglycemia events in the dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls (pooled RR 0.26; 95% CI [0.08, 0.82]; P overall effect = .02) (Fig. 5).

caption.p: Forest plot showing Hypoglycemia in the dapagliflozin treated group compared to controls.

sec.title: 5. Discussion
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy and safety of dapagliflozin in patients with DN, synthesizing data from 2 studies involving 296 participants. The findings indicate that dapagliflozin significantly improves renal function and glycemic control, as evidenced by the reductions in serum creatinine and HbA1c levels compared to placebo. However, no significant changes were observed in the UACR, and the treatment group exhibited a lower incidence of hypoglycemia.

Dapagliflozin demonstrated a notable reduction in serum creatinine levels, suggesting a potential renoprotective effect. This finding aligns with previous studies indicating that SGLT2 inhibitors can slow the progression of kidney disease in patients with type 2 diabetes.[3,5] The mechanism behind this protective effect may involve the reduction of intraglomerular pressure through the inhibition of SGLT2, leading to improved renal hemodynamics and a decrease in hyperfiltration.[14] The significant reduction in HbA1c observed in the dapagliflozin group confirms its efficacy in improving glycemic control. This is consistent with the well-documented glucose-lowering effects of SGLT2 inhibitors.[15,16] Improved glycemic control is crucial in managing DN, as sustained hyperglycemia is a primary driver of kidney damage in diabetes.[17] Contrary to the significant improvements in serum creatinine and HbA1c, our analysis did not find a statistically significant reduction in UACR. This result may be due to the limited number of studies and participants included in our meta-analysis. Previous larger trials have shown that dapagliflozin and other SGLT2 inhibitors can reduce albuminuria, a marker of kidney damage.[18] Further research with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods is necessary to elucidate the impact of dapagliflozin on UACR in DN patients.

The safety analysis revealed a lower incidence of hypoglycemia in the dapagliflozin group compared to placebo. This is consistent with the mechanism of SGLT2 inhibitors, which lower blood glucose levels without stimulating insulin secretion, thereby reducing the risk of hypoglycemia.[2] Additionally, the adverse event profile was similar between the dapagliflozin and placebo groups, suggesting that dapagliflozin is well-tolerated in patients with DN.

The pathogenesis of DN is very complex and is still not fully understood.[19] Numerous routes and mediators are implicated in the onset and development of diabetic kidney disease,[20] including angiotensin II, oxidative stress, and inflammatory processes, which are now thought to be significant contributors.[21] Our meta-analysis successfully demonstrated the dapagliflozin as potential therapeutic measures that can be used in the treatment of DN with good safety profile. However, further large-scale studies are warranted to understand the pathophysiology of DN and role of Dapagliflozin.

sec.title: 5.1. Limitations
sec.p: Several limitations should be acknowledged in this review. First, the number of included studies and participants was relatively small, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Second, the heterogeneity in study design, population characteristics, and duration of follow-up might have influenced the outcomes. Third, the review relied on published data, and potential publication bias can not be excluded. Additionally, variations in baseline UACR and eGFR between studies may contribute to heterogeneity. Despite these limitations, our findings provide valuable insights into the potential benefits and safety of dapagliflozin in DN.

sec.title: 6. Conclusions
sec.p: This systematic review and meta-analysis suggest that dapagliflozin is effective in improving renal function and glycemic control in patients with DN, with a favorable safety profile. However, its impact on albuminuria remains unclear. These findings support the use of dapagliflozin as a therapeutic option in managing DN but underscore the need for larger, multi-center RCTs with longer follow-up periods to confirm these results and further explore the long-term renal and cardiovascular benefits of dapagliflozin.
